items.text: I’ll map the repository first, then read the entry points, runtime flow, and each source/config file to write a detailed reverse-engineering document that reflects how this project actually works.

The repository has two distinct application paths: a newer local browser automation dashboard and an older Express/MongoDB job-hunting service that can also deploy to Vercel. I’m tracing both so the document will explain the actual boundaries and point out places where the README and code differ.

I’ve confirmed the local mode is selected dynamically by `src/index.js`: with a local profile and no MongoDB/Vercel flag, `npm start` serves the local automation dashboard; otherwise it loads the multi-user MongoDB application. I’m writing the document around that split and covering every tracked source file by responsibility, with the large company catalogs summarized as data rather than dumping their rows into prose.

+# JobHunter: reverse-engineering guide
+
+**Repository reviewed:** 12 November 2026. This document describes the code and configuration currently in this checkout. It is a static code-reading guide; no test suite, live browser, database, mail account, or external job board was run as part of preparing it.
+
+## 1. What this project is
+
+JobHunter contains two related but operationally different systems:
+
+1. **Local personal automation** — a single-user Express dashboard, Playwright browser worker, local JSON data store, candidate profile, ATS connectors, Gmail IMAP integration, and reports. Its entry point is `src/automation/server.js`.
+2. **Legacy multi-user service** — an Express API backed by MongoDB, JWT authentication, resume parsing, public job scrapers, match scoring, user applications, email/Telegram notifications, and serverless/Vercel routes. Its entry point is the main body of `src/index.js`.
+
+`src/index.js` selects local mode when `VERCEL` is unset, `MONGODB_URI` is unset, and `.automation/profile.json` exists. Otherwise it loads the MongoDB service. `npm run automation` always starts the local automation server directly. `npm start` runs `src/index.js`, so its behavior depends on environment and local files. The local data model is separate from the Mongoose models; there is no code path that synchronizes the two stores.
+
+The package manifest describes an automated job-hunting system, but the local worker is the more feature-rich and current workflow. README statements and platform notes are not uniformly aligned with connectors currently present in code; see §8.
+
+## 2. Runtime and data-flow map
+
+### Local automation
+
+```text
+public/automation.html
+        │ fetch /api/*
+src/automation/server.js ── cron schedules ── src/automation/runner.js
+                                                ├─ discovery.js ─ companies.js / ATS boards
+                                                ├─ matching.js ─ profile + history/rules
+                                                ├─ browser.js ─ ATS-specific adapters
+                                                │                ├─ workday.js
+                                                │                ├─ naukri.js
+                                                │                ├─ linkedin.js
+                                                │                ├─ wellfound.js
+                                                │                └─ hirist.js
+                                                ├─ answers.js ─ profile + saved answers
+                                                ├─ inbox.js / email.js / linkedinAlerts.js ─ Gmail IMAP
+                                                └─ reports.js / shortlist.js
+All local private state and artifacts → .automation/ (or AUTOMATION_DATA_DIR)
+```
+
+Typical run: load profile → recover interrupted attempts → re-evaluate and de-duplicate queue → optionally sync/search Naukri at configured quiet hours → check Gmail-derived alerts and Wellfound → perform the daily company career sweep when due → evaluate fresh jobs → fill forms → record submission evidence/status → scan replies → save reports. The runner uses a lock and a per-run state record. An interrupted `filling`/`submitting` job becomes `submission_uncertain`, which requires reconciliation and is intentionally excluded from automatic retries.
+
+The central local job states include `queued`, `filling`, `submitted`, `needs_input`, `submission_uncertain`, `excluded`, and `archived`. `submitted` is intended to mean a site confirmation was observed, not merely that a button was clicked. Matching includes posting freshness (seven days), salary/location/employment eligibility, exclusions, duplicate-role detection, and a two-per-company ceiling. Queue selection balances company categories and ranks candidates.
+
+### Legacy MongoDB service
+
+```text
+public/index.html → /api routes (src/routes.js) → src/models.js (Mongoose)
+                                     ├─ src/runner.js
+                                     │   ├─ scrapers/jobScraper.js
+                                     │   ├─ scrapers/companyScraper.js
+                                     │   ├─ scrapers/jobEnricher.js
+                                     │   ├─ parsers/resumeParser.js
+                                     │   └─ matchers/jobMatcher.js
+                                     ├─ notifiers/notifier.js
+                                     └─ notifiers/telegramBot.js
+```
+
+The service stores users, resumes, jobs, applications and reports in MongoDB. Its daily runner gathers from job boards and career boards, scores against an extracted resume profile, persists jobs and creates application records/notifications. The route layer exposes authentication, job lists/filters, resume upload, run control, application state, exports, analytics, notification preferences, Telegram linking, Naukri sync, and company config.
+
+### Deployment entry points
+
+`vercel.json` maps `/api/*` to serverless handlers or the legacy `src/index.js`, serves static files from `public/`, and schedules `/api/cron` at `30 2 * * *` UTC (08:00 India time). `api/cron.js` runs the legacy multi-user scraper flow; it does not start the local Playwright automation worker. `src/index.js` avoids local cron and bot polling under Vercel. Deployment requires environment variables and a reachable MongoDB service.
+
+## 3. Local state, profile, and configuration
+
+`src/automation/store.js` resolves the data root to `AUTOMATION_DATA_DIR`, or `.automation/` at the repository root. It reads/writes named JSON files, creates the root with restrictive directory/file modes, and writes through a temporary file followed by rename. The main `state.json` holds jobs, runs, events, saved question answers, exclusions and settings. Additional files are created for profile, browser sessions, Gmail connection, platform status, and other integration data. Reports and screenshots/evidence live below the same private root. `.gitignore` and `.vercelignore` exclude `.automation/`, uploads, secrets and resume files.
+
+`profile.example.json` is the local automation profile template. Its fields feed form answers and eligibility: identity/contact, current employer/title/experience, compensation and notice period, cities/remote country, skills and years, education/employment history, standing answers, resume filename/text, permissions, search terms, and cover letter. The worker should only submit confirmed candidate facts. `authorized` expresses configured permissions, but individual connectors may still stop at account walls, unsupported questions, CAPTCHA, or unverified upload/submission stages.
+
+`config.json` is a legacy service company preference/block list and is ignored by Git. `.env.example` documents environment variables for MongoDB, Telegram/email notification, server ports, resume path and limits, local worker, browser channel, and optional Workday credentials. `.env` is ignored; its contents were intentionally not included in this document. The local Gmail IMAP app password is entered through the dashboard and persisted in the private local store. `package-lock.json` pins dependency resolution; it is generated package metadata rather than application logic.
+

+
+## 5. Important boundaries and design rules
+
+- **Two independent persistence/security models.** Local automation stores personal profile, answers, session state and Gmail credential in filesystem JSON. Legacy mode stores multi-user records in MongoDB and uses JWT authentication. Do not assume local profile or job history appears in MongoDB or vice versa.
+- **Discovery is not application.** Company and LinkedIn-alert leads may be stale or merely indexed; the dashboard/shortlist records evidence level and manual action. A submitted state should have site confirmation evidence.
+- **Unknown answers should block.** `answers.js` and connector-specific checks avoid guessing legal consent and facts. Saved answers are scoped so one employer/site/question cannot silently authorize another context.
+- **Uncertain submit is a special state.** Network loss after submit can make outcome ambiguous. The runner avoids retrying it automatically to prevent duplicate applications; use dashboard reconciliation after checking the site.
+- **External integrations have different trust boundaries.** Legacy SMTP/Telegram notifications are distinct from local Gmail IMAP reply reading and ATS verification-code lookup.
+- **Catalog data is not proof of vacancy.** A company-board slug can fail, and a company career URL or search result can be stale. Validate connector data independently before relying on coverage claims.
+
+## 6. How to navigate a change
+
+For a local worker change, start at the dashboard action/API route, trace into `runner.js`, then `matching.js`/`discovery.js`/`browser.js`, and inspect the connector for a site-specific flow. Check `answers.js` before adding automatic answers; answers should be based on explicit profile data or saved user input. Check persistence and report side effects in `store.js` and `reports.js`.
+
+For a legacy service change, trace `src/routes.js` → `src/runner.js` → scrapers/parser/matcher → `src/models.js` and notifier. Keep user filters scoped by authenticated `userId`; review the separate serverless route when changing behavior intended for Vercel.
+
+The repository includes `npm test` and `npm run automation:check`, but this review intentionally did not execute either. The former is the unit/browser test suite. The latter is an operational connector inspection script whose flags can open browsers or mutate local job state.
+
+## 7. Runtime prerequisites
+
+- Node.js compatible with the installed dependencies (README requests Node 18+), `npm install`; Playwright Chromium/browser installation for local browser automation.
+- Local automation: candidate profile at `.automation/profile.json`; keep the host awake for scheduled work; optional Gmail app password for inbox tracking and Workday credentials for Workday account flows.
+- Legacy service: MongoDB connection, optional SMTP/Telegram credentials, and a resume upload/profile for useful matching.
+- Vercel legacy scheduler: deployment environment must include database and any required secrets; serverless execution does not provide the always-on local browser session expected by personal automation.
+
+## 8. Notable discrepancies and review findings
+
+These are observations from static reading, not runtime verification:
+
+1. **README platform claims are stale/inconsistent.** It says LinkedIn is turned off and should be done manually; code has a LinkedIn connector and alert-email ingestion, while `skipAts: ['linkedin']` disables it by default. README also describes Naukri as automatically applied in night windows, while `companies.js` platform notes describe Naukri as manual and say unattended portal submission is not enabled. The actual `runner.js` invokes Naukri sync/discovery during quiet hours; connector code determines precisely what actions are active.
+2. **README OS guidance conflicts with environment.** README setup says Mac and browser sleep advice; this checkout is being worked on under Windows. Paths and process/browser behavior should be checked on the target host before treating Mac-only instructions as universal.
+3. **`npm start` mode is implicit.** Presence of a local `.automation/profile.json` with no `MONGODB_URI` switches it to local automation. A developer expecting the legacy app may start the wrong service; use `npm run automation` for explicit local mode and configure the legacy DB/environment explicitly.
+4. **Legacy API deployment has diagnostic endpoints.** `api/debug.js` returns connection readiness and a shortened Mongo URI prefix; `api/dbtest.js` returns collection names. Review whether these endpoints should remain publicly routable in production.
+5. **Vercel cron auth condition is permissive when `VERCEL` is set.** `api/cron.js` rejects a bad/missing cron bearer token only when `VERCEL` is not set. This appears opposite to the comment's stated intent to verify the Vercel cron secret and warrants a focused security review before deployment.
+6. **TLS certificate validation is disabled in legacy Mongo connection paths for SRV URIs.** Both `src/index.js` and `api/cron.js` set `tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: true`; that weakens server identity verification and should be reviewed for production.
+7. **Large inline UI/catalog files raise maintenance cost.** `public/automation.html` combines frontend logic and presentation, while `companyLists.js`/`companyFixes.js` are broad data sources. Changes benefit from focused tests and data provenance checks.
+8. **The daily schedules are separate.** Local automation schedules multiple night runs plus a morning run and inbox scans; Vercel cron runs a legacy scrape pipeline daily. They do not share a queue or application history.
+
+## 9. Glossary
+
+- **ATS:** Applicant tracking system, such as Greenhouse, Lever, SmartRecruiters or Workday.
+- **Discovery:** Finding and normalizing a job posting; it does not mean applying.
+- **Needs input:** A required question, account login, verification or unsupported form step needs user action.
+- **Submission uncertain:** The worker cannot establish whether submission succeeded; manually reconcile before retry.
+- **Evidence:** Confirmation text, response metadata or screenshot that supports an application state.
+- **Company sweep:** The local worker's scan across its configured company career boards.

content.text: How to initialize candidate  profile

items.text:
The worker can’t start because it expects a profile at `.automation/profile.json`. Create it from the example, then replace the placeholders with your real information:

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .automation
Copy-Item profile.example.json .automation/profile.json
notepad .automation/profile.json
```

At minimum, update your name, email, phone, current role and employer, experience, preferred locations, search keywords, and resume details. Set `resumeFile` to your resume’s filename and place that file in `.automation`. Check `standingAnswers` carefully and enter only truthful answers.

Save the file, then run:

```powershell
npm run automation
```

The profile contains personal data, so keep it in `.automation` and don’t share or commit it.

content.text: Is there any way so user get automatted their profile using UI ?

items.text:
Yes. A UI could let a user upload a PDF or DOCX resume, extract candidate details, show them in an editable review form, and save the confirmed profile locally.

That flow **isn’t currently implemented** in the local dashboard: its “Profile & rules” tab displays profile details and lets you change the daily target, but doesn’t provide profile editing or resume upload. The legacy resume parser exists, but it saves data to the MongoDB service; it doesn’t populate `.automation/profile.json`.

A good setup flow would be **upload → extract → review/edit → save**. The review step matters because resumes often don’t specify things like salary expectations, notice period, or years per skill. Those fields should stay blank until the user confirms them.

+### Local worker run order
+
+`runner.run()` acquires the filesystem lock, recovers stale `filling`/`submitting` jobs into `submission_uncertain`, requires a saved profile, records a run entry, and re-evaluates existing queue items. Connector-specific failures are often caught and converted to events so one external source does not abort the whole run.

+# Cold Email Contact Storage Plan
+
+## Goal
+
+Persist email contacts extracted from spreadsheets, show them in the Cold email tab after reloads and restarts, let the user select saved contacts for a future campaign, and prevent duplicate email records.
+
+This document is a design plan only. It does not change the application.
+
+## Current behavior and architecture
+
+- The Cold email page is served by the local automation service in `src/automation/server.js`.
+- Spreadsheet parsing in `src/automation/coldEmail.js` extracts addresses and returns them to the browser. The selected list currently exists only in page memory; it is not saved.
+- The local automation service persists user data as JSON under `.automation/` (or `AUTOMATION_DATA_DIR`) through `src/automation/store.js`.
+- The MongoDB models in `src/models.js` belong to the separate, multi-user legacy dashboard. The local automation server does not connect to MongoDB or authenticate a MongoDB user.
+
+## Storage recommendation
+
+For the current Cold email feature, store contacts in the local automation data directory using the existing JSON store. This keeps imported addresses on the same computer as the local profile and Gmail credentials, and does not make the local-only feature depend on the legacy MongoDB service.
+
+Use a new `company-contacts.json` store file, accessed through `store.read('company-contacts', [])` and `store.write('company-contacts', records)`. The existing store writes JSON through a temporary file and rename. Keep this separate from `state.json` so a growing address book does not inflate the frequently polled dashboard state.
+
+If “database” specifically means MongoDB or a contacts list shared between devices/users, that is a different architecture decision: it requires account ownership, authenticated local-to-remote API calls, deployment configuration, and a privacy/retention policy. Do not silently put locally imported contacts into the legacy database.
+
+## Contact record
+
+```json
+{
+  "id": "stable UUID",
+  "email": "Jane.Doe@example.com",
+  "emailNormalized": "jane.doe@example.com",
+  "name": "Jane Doe",
+  "companies": ["Example Technologies"],
+  "sourceFiles": ["contacts.xlsx"],
+  "firstImportedAt": "ISO-8601 timestamp",
+  "lastImportedAt": "ISO-8601 timestamp",
+  "importCount": 1,
+  "status": "active"
+}
+```
+
+`name` and company association are optional. Do not store message bodies, attachments, Gmail credentials, or campaign send logs in the contact record. Preserve the first-seen timestamp and ID on repeat imports; update `lastImportedAt`, `importCount`, and any new company/source associations.
+
+## Duplicate policy
+
+Use `emailNormalized` as the global unique key for a contact:
+
+1. Trim surrounding whitespace and lowercase the address for comparison.
+2. Validate the normalized address before accepting it.
+3. Deduplicate the spreadsheet preview by normalized address.
+4. On import, upsert by normalized email. Re-importing the same address updates the existing record instead of creating a second one.
+5. If the same address appears under another company, retain one contact and add that company to its `companies` list. Do not create another selectable recipient row.
+6. Deduplicate selected recipient IDs/emails again on the server immediately before sending.
+
+This is a global policy: the same mailbox associated with multiple companies appears once in the address book, with multiple company labels. If the product later needs a separate person/contact record per company, change the unique key to `(companyKey, emailNormalized)` intentionally and update the acceptance criteria.
+
+## Spreadsheet import changes
+
+The current extractor returns a flat address list. Extend it to produce row-based import candidates:
+
+- `email`
+- optional `name`
+- optional `company`
+- source worksheet and row number for preview/debugging
+
+Recognize common column names such as `email`, `email address`, `company`, `organization`, `employer`, `name`, and `contact`. Keep the existing scan-any-cell behavior as a fallback for sheets without headers. Continue supporting `.xlsx` and `.csv`; report unsupported files and invalid addresses without failing the whole import.
+
+The UI should show a preview and import summary before saving: new contacts, already-known addresses, rows with invalid addresses, and addresses without a company value. Saving should not send email.
+
+## API plan
+
+Add these local, token-protected mutation/read routes in `src/automation/server.js`:
+
+| Route | Purpose |
+|---|---|
+| `GET /api/cold-email/contacts?query=&company=&status=active` | Return saved contacts for the Cold email address book, with paging and search. |
+| `POST /api/cold-email/contacts/import` | Validate and upsert extracted candidates; return created/updated/duplicate/invalid counts. |
+| `PATCH /api/cold-email/contacts/:id` | Edit the display name, company associations, or active/archive state. |
+| `DELETE /api/cold-email/contacts/:id` | Permanently remove a contact after user confirmation. |
+
+The current `/api/cold-email/extract` remains a preview/parser route. Keep sending asynchronous as it is today, but update the send request to submit selected contact IDs. The server must resolve those IDs to active saved contacts, re-deduplicate addresses, then create one message per recipient. Never trust a client-provided company label or email when a saved contact ID is available.
+
+## Cold email UI plan
+
+Add a **Saved contacts** section above the compose form:
+
+- Search by email, name, or company.
+- Filter by company and active/archive state.
+- Display name, email, company labels, and last imported date.
+- Select individual contacts or all visible results; display the unique selected-recipient count.
+- Provide edit, archive, and delete actions.
+- Keep the spreadsheet preview/import controls separate from the saved address book.
+- Compose subject, body, and attachment as today; show the selected recipients before the final send confirmation.
+
+After importing, refresh the saved contacts list and allow the new records to be selected immediately. When the page is reopened, load contacts from the local API rather than relying on browser memory or `sessionStorage`.
+
+## Privacy, safety, and operational limits
+
+- Contact data remains in `.automation/` and is excluded from Git, reports, and the MongoDB legacy app.
+- Keep spreadsheet and attachment upload limits; do not persist uploaded files after parsing or sending.
+- Use the existing loopback-only server and `X-JobHunter-Token` requirement for every mutation.
+- Make import idempotent and keep duplicate prevention on the server, not only in browser code.
+- Provide a clear delete action and document that a backup of `.automation/` may contain the contact database.
+- Sending must continue to use the connected Gmail account, individual recipient messages, recipient review, authorization confirmation, and a final send confirmation.
+
+## Implementation phases
+
+1. Define the record shape, validation rules, normalized-email upsert helper, and import summary.
+2. Add persistent local contact storage and list/import/edit/archive/delete endpoints.
+3. Change spreadsheet extraction to retain row/company/name context and create a reviewable import preview.
+4. Add the Saved contacts UI, search/filter, selection, and import summary.
+5. Change campaign submission to resolve selected saved contact IDs server-side and show progress/results against those contacts.
+6. Add tests for extraction and deduplication, persistence after reload, repeated imports, company association merging, invalid addresses, and send-time duplicate filtering.
+
+## Acceptance criteria
+
+- A newly imported contact remains visible after page reload and automation-server restart.
+- Re-importing `Jane.Doe@example.com`, ` jane.doe@example.com `, or `JANE.DOE@EXAMPLE.COM` creates no additional record.
+- An address found in multiple rows, sheets, or files remains one selectable contact.
+- New company associations are added to the existing record without duplicating its email.
+- Invalid email values are reported and never saved or sent.
+- The UI can search and select saved addresses, and the server sends only the selected active contacts.
+- Campaign sending still sends one email per address, and duplicate selected contacts cannot cause duplicate messages.
+- No contact email is written to `state.json`, application reports, or the legacy MongoDB database.

+# Multi-user portal and automation architecture
+
+## Purpose
+
+This document describes how to evolve Naukri Khojo from its current single-user local automation worker into a service for many portal accounts. It is a design and implementation plan; it does not change application behavior.
+
+## Current architecture and limit
+
+The main portal authenticates users with MongoDB-backed accounts and JWTs. Its jobs, resumes, applications, and reports are generally filtered by `userId`.
+
+Automation is a separate local Express service. It stores one profile, one job state, platform sessions, email settings, contacts, and reports in `.automation/` (or one configured `AUTOMATION_DATA_DIR`). It also has one runner/browser instance and a single worker lock. `portal-owner.json` binds that directory to one portal account and blocks other accounts to prevent data exposure.
+
+This protects the current local setup, but it does not provide shared multi-user automation. Do not remove the owner check or let several users share one `.automation` directory. That would expose resumes, credentials, job history, and browser sessions across accounts.
+
+## Recommended target
+
+Keep the Vercel app as the authenticated web/API layer. Move long-running automation to a separate worker service backed by shared persistent infrastructure:
+
+```text
+Browser
+  | authenticated portal API (JWT)
+  v
+Portal API / Vercel functions ---- MongoDB (user-owned records)
+  | enqueue job with userId
+  v
+Durable queue (Redis/BullMQ or managed equivalent)
+  | claim one task with lease + idempotency key
+  v
+Automation worker containers
+  | isolated browser context and secrets for one user/task
+  +---- MongoDB (job state, profile references, outcomes)
+  +---- Private object storage (resume files, evidence, attachments)
+```
+
+Vercel functions should authenticate requests, validate input, read/write short operations, and enqueue work. They should not own browser sessions, scheduler state, or long-running application runs. Workers should be deployable separately and scale independently from web requests.
+
+## Data ownership and records
+
+Every user-created or user-visible record must have an immutable `userId` owner. Enforce the owner in database queries and in service-layer functions; never rely on the client to provide a trusted owner ID.
+
+Recommended record groups:
+
+| Data | Suggested storage | Ownership and notes |
+|---|---|---|
+| Account and authentication | MongoDB `User` | Existing account ID remains the owner key. Never expose password hashes. |
+| Candidate profile and preferences | MongoDB `CandidateProfile` (or an expanded profile document) | Unique index on `userId`; use an explicit merge policy for fields imported from the existing `Resume` record. |
+| Resume documents | Private object storage plus MongoDB metadata | Store object key, owner, content type, size, checksum, and timestamps. Do not store public URLs. |
+| Jobs and applications | Existing MongoDB models, migrated/retained with `userId` | Add compound indexes for common owner queries and idempotency keys. |
+| Automation run/task | MongoDB `AutomationRun` plus durable queue | Fields include `userId`, task type, status, attempts, lease, timestamps, and idempotency key. |
+| Portal sessions | Existing JWT/session system | Require a stable hosted `JWT_SECRET`; do not use process-random secrets in serverless deployments. |
+| Platform/Gmail credentials | Secret manager or encrypted credential store | Encrypt with a KMS-managed key; decrypt only inside the worker for the owning user. Never put secrets in job payloads/logs. |
+| Contact book and cold email | MongoDB collection keyed by `userId` | Unique compound key `{ userId, emailNormalized }`; campaigns reference owned contact IDs. |
+| Reports and evidence | MongoDB metadata + private object storage | Every read/download checks `userId`; use short-lived signed URLs after authorization. |
+
+Do not copy `portalUserId` into one global local JSON file and treat that as multi-tenancy. A single owner marker is an intentional one-account lock, not a scalable ownership model.
+
+## Authentication and request isolation
+
+1. Keep the existing portal login and JWT flow as the entry point.
+2. On every authenticated API route, derive `userId` from the verified token (`req.user._id`). Ignore or reject client-supplied `userId` values.
+3. Scope reads, updates, deletes, exports, and status lookups by both record ID and authenticated `userId`, for example `findOne({ _id: id, userId: req.user._id })`.
+4. Queue messages include `userId` and a record ID, but workers re-load the record with an owner-scoped query before execution.
+5. Use short-lived, one-purpose worker credentials or internal service authentication. Never send the user's portal JWT, password, Gmail app password, or platform cookies in a queue message.
+6. Protect uploaded files, reports, screenshots, and cold-email contacts with the same ownership checks as API records.
+7. Rate-limit login per account and IP with a shared store (Redis or gateway), not an in-memory map in each serverless instance.
+
+## Worker isolation and concurrency
+
+- A task is claimed atomically with a lease, owner ID, and idempotency key. A worker crash allows lease expiry and safe recovery.
+- Never retry an application submission when its outcome is uncertain. Require reconciliation before another submit attempt, matching the existing worker safety behavior.
+- Use a separate browser context and temporary download directory per task/user. Do not share cookies, local storage, profile directories, or browser pages between users.
+- Enforce one active automation run per user initially. Different users may run concurrently, subject to a global worker capacity limit.
+- Limit workers globally and per user; bound browser memory/CPU, timeouts, queue depth, attachment size, and retries.
+- Store no process-local scheduler as the source of truth. Use a durable scheduler/queue and distributed locks so multiple worker replicas cannot enqueue duplicate daily runs.
+- Ensure temporary resume and evidence files are deleted after upload or retention expiry. Define a retention policy before launch.
+
+## Profile synchronization policy
+
+Choose one source of truth for each field before implementing bidirectional sync.
+
+- Portal `User` is authoritative for account email and account ID.
+- The user's resume/profile record is authoritative for imported name, skills, experience, roles, and resume text.
+- Automation-only preferences (cities, salary, notice period, authorized submission choices, and platform connections) remain in the candidate profile unless and until the main portal has corresponding fields.
+- Merge only fields that are present and validated. An absent resume value must not erase an existing user-entered automation value.
+- Keep an audit timestamp/source for imported fields so users can see when profile data was synchronized.
+- Never infer consent or enable automatic submission from login or resume import.
+
+## Migration plan
+
+### Phase 1: ownership audit and schema preparation
+
+- Audit every route and report/export for owner-scoped queries.
+- Add/confirm `userId` fields and compound indexes for profiles, contacts, runs, and any state currently held only in JSON.
+- Add migration tooling that maps existing records to the currently linked portal account only after verifying the current `portal-owner` and profile binding.
+- Keep the local worker behavior unchanged during this phase.
+
+### Phase 2: profile, contact, and credential persistence
+
+- Move candidate profile and company contacts from the global JSON store to user-owned MongoDB collections.
+- Move resume/evidence files to private object storage and retain metadata in MongoDB.
+- Encrypt Gmail and platform credentials using a managed key; implement per-user credential read/write operations.
+- Keep a temporary, explicit export/backup path for a user's existing `.automation` data before migration.
+
+### Phase 3: run queue and worker service
+
+- Add authenticated `POST /api/automation/runs` to validate user state and enqueue a run.
+- Add `GET /api/automation/runs/:id` scoped by user ID for progress/results.
+- Add durable queue processing, per-user run locks, global concurrency limits, retries, cancellation, and crash recovery.
+- Refactor automation modules to receive a user-scoped context (profile, settings, state, credentials, storage) as arguments instead of importing a process-global `store` singleton.
+- Keep the browser process/context isolated for each active task.
+
+### Phase 4: UI and account migration
+
+- Replace the local SSO handoff with the portal's authenticated run/status API for hosted automation.
+- Show the active account, queue status, run history, and per-user settings in the portal UI.
+- Provide a user-reviewed import flow from `.automation/` for existing local profiles, jobs, contacts, and settings. Do not automatically merge one local user's history into another account.
+- Retain `npm run automation` as a local single-user mode if desired, clearly separate from hosted multi-user mode.
+
+### Phase 5: staged load and isolation validation
+
+- Start with read-only/API load, then login and profile reads, then queue operations, and only later controlled browser dry runs.
+- Run 1, 10, 25, 50, and 100 virtual users; measure p50/p95/p99 latency, errors, Mongo connection pool saturation, queue wait, worker CPU/memory, and completion time.
+- Use synthetic accounts and fake/test applications. Do not use production resumes, real platform accounts, or real email sends in load tests.
+- Include cross-account penetration checks: user A must not fetch user B's profile, resume, job, contact, campaign, report, file, run ID, or credentials by changing an ID.
+
+## Acceptance criteria for 100-user readiness
+
+- 100 users can sign in and use dashboard APIs concurrently without sharing data.
+- All user-owned collections and files enforce ownership in the backend, including exports and direct-download routes.
+- Each user sees only their own profile, resumes, contacts, jobs, runs, campaigns, reports, and platform connections.
+- One user's queued or failed job cannot modify another user's state or block their worker lock.
+- A worker restart does not lose queued tasks or duplicate an application submission.
+- Worker replicas can scale horizontally without duplicate scheduling or shared browser sessions.
+- Per-user and global concurrency limits behave predictably at 100 users; overload returns a clear queued/rate-limited state rather than corrupting state.
+- A 100-user synthetic load test meets agreed latency/error/resource targets and passes cross-account isolation checks.
+
+## Current deployment decision
+
+The current Vercel configuration serves the web/API layer and cron endpoint. The browser automation service is a separate loopback-only Node process and local filesystem store. Uploading the current repository to Vercel does not turn that local process into a multi-user automation service. Keep the current one-account owner guard until the user-scoped storage and worker queue are implemented and validated.
